entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.2.1">2Sa 23:1-2   1</reference>  Divine saying of David the son of Jesse, <div eID="gen4646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4647" type="x-p"/> Divine saying of the man, the highly exalted, <div eID="gen4647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> Of the anointed of the God of Jacob, <div eID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4649" type="x-p"/> And of the lovely one in the songs of praise of Israel.   2  The Spirit of Jehovah speaks through me, <div eID="gen4649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4650" type="x-p"/> And His word is upon my tongue. <div eID="gen4650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4651" type="x-p"/> This introduction to the prophetic announcement rests, both as to form and substance, upon the last sayings of Balaam concerning the future history of Israel (Num 24:3, Num 24:15). This not only shows to what extent David had occupied himself with the utterances of the earlier men of God concerning Israel’s future; but indicates, at the same time, that his own prophetic utterance was intended to be a further expansion of Balaam’s prophecy concerning the Star out of Jacob and the Sceptre out of Israel. Like Balaam, he calls his prophecy a נאם, i.e., a <hi type="italic">divine saying</hi> or oracle, as a revelation which he had received directly from God (see at Num 24:3). But the recipient of this revelation was not, like Balaam the son of Beor, a man with closed eye, whose eyes had been opened by a vision of the Almighty, but “<hi type="italic">the man who was raised up on high</hi>” (על, adverbially “<hi type="italic">above</hi>,” is, strictly speaking, a substantive, “<hi type="italic">height</hi>,” used in an adverbial sense, as in Hos 11:7, and probably also <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:16</reference>), i.e., whom God had lifted up out of humiliation to be the ruler of His people, yea, even to be the head of the nations (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">2Sa 22:44</reference>). Luther’s rendering, “who is assured of the Messiah of the God of Jacob,” is based upon the Vulgate, “<hi type="italic">cui constitutum est de Christo Dei Jacob</hi>,” and cannot be grammatically sustained. David was exalted on the one hand as “<hi type="italic">the anointed of the God of Jacob</hi>,” i.e., as the one whom the God of Israel had anointed king over His people, and on the other hand as “the lovely one in Israel’s songs of praise,” i.e., the man whom God had enabled to sing lovely songs of praise in celebration of His grace and glory. זמיר = זמרה does not mean a song generally, but a song of praise in honour of God (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>), like מזמור in the headings to the psalms. As David on the one hand had firmly established the kingdom of God in an earthly and political respect as the anointed of Jehovah, i.e., as king, so had he on the other, as the composer of Israel’s songs of praise, promoted the spiritual edification of that kingdom. The idea of נאם is explained in 2Sa 23:2. The Spirit of Jehovah speaks through him; his words are the inspiration of God. The preterite דּבּר relates to the divine inspiration which preceded the utterance of the divine saying. בּ דּבּר, literally to speak into a person, as in Hos 1:2. The saying itself commences with 2Sa 23:3.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">2Sa 22:3</reference>   <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">3</reference>  The God of Israel saith, <div eID="gen4651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4652" type="x-p"/> The Rock of Israel speaketh to me: <div eID="gen4652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4653" type="x-p"/> A Ruler over men, just, <div eID="gen4653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4654" type="x-p"/> A Ruler in the fear of God.   4  And as light of the morning, when the sun rises, <div eID="gen4654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> As morning without clouds: <div eID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4656" type="x-p"/> From shining out of rain (springeth) green out of the earth.   5  For is not my house thus with God? <div eID="gen4656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4657" type="x-p"/> For He hath made me an everlasting covenant, <div eID="gen4657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> Provided with all, and attested; <div eID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4659" type="x-p"/> For all my salvation and all good pleasure, <div eID="gen4659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4660" type="x-p"/> Should He then not cause it to grow? <div eID="gen4660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> As the prophets generally preface their saying with “thus saith the Lord,” so David commences his prophetic saying with “<hi type="italic">the God of Israel saith</hi>,” for the purpose of describing it most emphatically as the word of God. He designates God “<hi type="italic">the God</hi>” and “<hi type="italic">The Rock</hi>” (as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">2Sa 22:3</reference>) of Israel, to indicate that the contents of his prophecy relate to the salvation of the people of Israel, and are guaranteed by the unchangeableness of God. The saying which follows bears the impress of a divine oracle even in its enigmatical brevity. The verbs are wanting in the different sentences of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference></hi> and 2Sa 23:4. “<hi type="italic">A ruler over men</hi>,” sc., “will arise,” or there will be. בּאדם does not mean “among men,” but “<hi type="italic">over men;</hi>” for בּ is to be taken as with the verb משׁל, as denoting the object ruled over (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>, etc.). האדם does not mean certain men, but the human race, humanity. This ruler is “<hi type="italic">just</hi>” in the fullest sense of the word, as in the passages founded upon this, viz., <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>; Zec 9:9, and Psa 72:2. The justice of the ruler is founded in his “<hi type="italic">fear of God</hi>.” אלהים יראת is governed freely by מושׁל. (On the fact itself, see <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>-3.) The meaning is, “A ruler over the human race will arise, a just ruler, and will exercise his dominion in the spirit of the fear of God.”

The Rock of Israel speaketh to me:
A Ruler over men, just,
A Ruler in the fear of God. 4 And as light of the morning, when the sun rises,

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> describes the blessing that will proceed from this ruler. The idea that <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> should be connected with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference></hi> so as to form one period, in the sense of “when one rules justly over men (as I do), it is as when a morning becomes clear,” must be rejected, for the simple reason that it overlooks Nathan’s promise (2 Samuel 7) altogether, and weakens the force of the saying so solemnly introduced as the word of God. The ruler over men whom David sees in spirit, is not any one who rules righteously over men; nor is the seed of David to be regarded as a collective expression indicating a merely ideal personality, but, according to the Chaldee rendering, the Messiah himself, the righteous Shoot whom the Lord would raise up to David (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>), and who would execute righteousness and judgment upon earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer 33:15</reference>). <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> is to be taken by itself as containing an independent thought, and the connection between it and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference> must be gathered from the words themselves: the appearance (the rise) of this Ruler will be “<hi type="italic">as light of the morning, when the sun rises</hi>.” At the same time, the Messiah is not to be regarded as the subject to בּקר אור (the light of the morning), as though the ruler over men were compared with the morning light; but the subject compared to the morning light is intentionally left indefinite, according to the view adopted by Luther in his exposition, “In the time of the Messiah it will be like the light of the morning.” We are precluded from regarding the Messiah as the subject, by the fact that the comparison is instituted not with the sun, but with the morning dawn at the rising of the sun, whose vivifying effects upon nature are described in the second clause of the verse. The words שׁמשׁ יזרח are to be taken relatively, as a more distinct definition of the morning light. The clause which follows, “<hi type="italic">morning without clouds</hi>,” is parallel to the foregoing, and describes more fully the nature of the morning. The light of the rising sun on a cloudless morning is an image of the coming salvation. The rising sun awakens the germs of life in the bosom of nature, which had been slumbering through the darkness of the night. “The state of things before the coming of the ruler resembles the darkness of the night” (Hengstenberg). The verb is also wanting in the second hemistich. “<hi type="italic">From the shining from rain</hi> (is, comes) <hi type="italic">fresh green out of the earth</hi>.” נגהּ signifies the brightness of the rising sun; but, so far as the actual meaning is concerned, it relates to the salvation which attends the coming of the righteous ruler. ממּטר is either subordinate to מנּגהּ, or co-ordinate with it. In the former case, we should have to render the passage, “from the shining of the sun which proceeds out of rain,” or “from the shining after rain;” and the allusion would be to a cloudless morning, when the shining of the sun after a night’s rain stimulates the growth of the plants. In the latter case, we should have to render it “from the shining (and) from the rain;” and the reference would be to a cloudless morning, on which the vegetation springs up from the ground through sunshine followed by rain. Grammatically considered, the first view (? the second) is the easier of the two; nevertheless we regard the other (? the first) as the only admissible one, inasmuch as rain is not to be expected when the sun has risen with a cloudless sky. The rays of the sun, as it rises after a night of rain, strengthen the fresh green of the plants. The rain is therefore a figurative representation of blessing generally (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference>), and the green grass which springs up from the earth after the rain is an image of the blessings of the Messianic salvation (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">Isa 44:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>). <div eID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference>, Solomon takes these words of David as the basis of his comparison of the effects resulting from the government of the true Prince of peace to the coming down of the rain upon the mown grass.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference> <div eID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4663" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>, the prophecy concerning the coming of the just ruler is sustained by being raced back to the original promise in 2 Samuel 7, in which David had received a pledge of this. The first and last clauses of this verse can only be made to yield a meaning in harmony with the context, by being taken interrogatively: “<hi type="italic">for is not my house so with God?</hi>” The question is only indicated by the tone (לא כּי = הלא כּי: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.23">2Sa 19:23</reference>), as is frequently the case, even before clauses commencing with לּא (e.g., Hos 11:5; Mal 2:15 : cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §324, a.). לא־כן (not so) is explained by the following clause, though the כּי which follows is not to be taken in the sense of “<hi type="italic">that</hi>.” Each of the two clauses contains a distinct thought. That of the first is, “Does not my house stand in such a relation to God, that the righteous ruler will spring from it?” This is then explained in the second: “for He hath made an everlasting covenant with me.” David calls the promise in 2Sa 7:12., that God would establish his kingdom to his seed for ever, a covenant, because it involved a reciprocal relation-namely, that Jehovah would first of all found for David a permanent house, and then that the seed of David was to build the house of the Lord. This covenant is בכּל ערוּכה, “<hi type="italic">equipped</hi> (or <hi type="italic">provided</hi>) <hi type="italic">with all</hi>” that could help to establish it. David could found upon this the certainty, that God would cause all the salvation to spring forth which had been pledged to his house in the promise referred to. כּל־ישׁעי, “<hi type="italic">all my salvation</hi>,” i.e., all the salvation promised to me and to my house. כּל־חפץ, not “all my desire,” but “<hi type="italic">all the good pleasure</hi>” of God, i.e., all the saving counsel of God expressed in that covenant. The כּי before לא is an energetic repetition of the כּי which introduces the explanatory thought, in the sense of a firm assurance: “<hi type="italic">for all my salvation and all good pleasure, yea, should He not cause it to spring forth?</hi>”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6-2Sam.7.6">2Sa 23:6-7   6</reference>  But the worthless, as rejected thorns are they all; <div eID="gen4663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4664" type="x-p"/> For men do not take them in the hand.   7  And the man who touches them <div eID="gen4664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4665" type="x-p"/> Provides himself with iron and spear-shaft, <div eID="gen4665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4666" type="x-p"/> And they are utterly burned with fire where they dwell. <div eID="gen4666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4667" type="x-p"/> The development of salvation under the ruler in righteousness and the fear of God is accompanied by judgment upon the ungodly. The abstract בליּעל, <hi type="italic">worthlessness</hi>, is stronger than בליּעל אישׁ, the worthless man, and depicts the godless as personified worthlessness. מנד, in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> מנּד, the <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> of נוּד or נדד, literally “<hi type="italic">scared</hi>” or hunted away. This epithet does not apply to the thorns, so well as to the ungodly who are compared to thorns. The reference is to thorns that men root out, not to those which they avoid on account of their prickles. כּלּהם, an antiquated form for כּלּם (see Ewald, §247, <hi type="italic">d</hi>.). To root them out, or clean the ground of them, men do not lay hold of them with the bare hand; but “<hi type="italic">whoever would touch them equips himself</hi> (ימּלא, sc., ידו, to '<hi type="italic">fill the hand</hi>' with anything: 2Ki 9:24) <hi type="italic">with iron</hi>, i.e., with iron weapons, <hi type="italic">and spear-shaft</hi>” (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.7">1Sa 17:7</reference>). This expression also relates to the godless rather than to the thorns. They are consumed בּשּׁבת, “<hi type="italic">at the dwelling</hi>,” i.e., as Kimchi explains, at the place of their dwelling, the place where they grow. For בּשּׁבת cannot mean “on the spot” in the sense of without delay. The burning of the thorns takes place at the final judgment upon the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">Mat 13:30</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.39">2Sa 23:8-39</reference> <div eID="gen4667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4668" type="x-p"/> The following list of David’s heroes we also find in 1 Chron 11:10-47, and expanded at the end by sixteen names (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:41-47</reference>), and attached in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">1Ch 11:10</reference> to the account of the conquest of the fortress of Zion by the introduction of a special heading. According to this heading, the heroes named assisted David greatly in his kingdom, along with all Israel, to make him king, from which it is evident that the chronicler intended by this heading to justify his appending the list to the account of the election of David as king over all the tribes of Israel (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1">1Ch 11:1</reference>), and of the conquest of Zion, which followed immediately afterwards. In every other respect the two lists agree with one another, except that there are a considerable number of errors of the text, more especially in the names, which are frequently corrupt in both texts, to that the true reading cannot be determined with certainty. The heroes enumerated are divided into three classes. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> class consists of three, viz., <hi type="italic">Jashobeam</hi>, <hi type="italic">Eleazar</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Shammah</hi>, of whom certain brave deeds are related, by which they reached the first rank among David’s heroes (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.12">2Sa 23:8-12</reference>). They were followed by <hi type="italic">Abishai</hi> and <hi type="italic">Benaiah</hi>, who were in the <hi type="italic">second</hi> class, and who had also distinguished themselves above the rest by their brave deeds, though they did not come up to the first three (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18-2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:18-23</reference>). The others all belonged to the <hi type="italic">third</hi> class, which consisted of thirty-two men, of whom no particular heroic deeds are mentioned (vv. 24-39). Twelve of these, viz., the five belonging to the first two classes and seven of the third, were appointed by David commanders of the twelve detachments into which he divided the army, each detachment to serve for one month in the year (1 Chron 27). These heroes, among whom we do not find Joab the commander-in-chief of the whole of the forces, were the king’s aides-de-camp, and are called in this respect השּׁלשׁי (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>), though the term השּׁלשׁים (the <hi type="italic">thirty</hi>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.24">2Sa 23:24</reference>) was also a very customary one, as their number amounted to thirty in a round sum. It is possible that at first they may have numbered exactly thirty; for, from the very nature of the case, we may be sure than in the many wars in which David was engaged, other heroes must have arisen at different times, who would be received into the corps already formed. This will explain the addition of sixteen names in the Chronicles, whether the chronicler made us of a different list from that employed by the author of the books before us, and one belonging to a later age, or whether the author of our books merely restricted himself to a description of the corps in its earlier condition.  <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.12">2Sa 23:8-12</reference> <hi type="italic">Heroes of the first class</hi>. - The short heading to our text, with which the list in the Chronicles also beings (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference>), simply gives the name of these heroes. But instead of “the <hi type="italic">names</hi> of the mighty men,” we have in the Chronicles “the <hi type="italic">number</hi> of the mighty men.” This variation is all the more striking, from the fact that in the Chronicles the total number is not given at the close of the list as it is in our text. At the same time, it can hardly be a copyist’s error for מבחר (<hi type="italic">selection</hi>), as Bertheau supposes, but must be attributable to the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.24">2Sa 23:24</reference>, these heroes constituted a corps which was named from the number of which it originally consisted. The first, <hi type="italic">Jashobeam</hi>, is called “the chief of the thirty” in the Chronicles. Instead of ישׁבעם (<hi type="italic">Jashobeam</hi>), the reading in the Chronicles, we have here בּשּׁבת ישׁב (<hi type="italic">Josheb-basshebeth</hi>), unquestionably a spurious reading, which probably arose, according to Kennicott’s conjecture, from the circumstance that the last two letters of ישׁבעם were written in one MS under בּשּׁבת in the line above (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">2Sa 23:7</reference>), and a copyist took בשׁבת from that line by mistake for עם. The correctness of the reading <hi type="italic">Jashobeam</hi> is established by 1Ch 27:2. The word תּחכּמני is also faulty, and should be corrected, according to the Chronicles, into בּן־חכמוני (<hi type="italic">Ben-hachmoni</hi>); for the statement that Jashobeam was a son (or descendant) of the family of <hi type="italic">Hachmon</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.32">1Ch 27:32</reference>) can easily be reconciled with that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.2">1Ch 27:2</reference>, to the effect that he was a son of Zabdiel. Instead of השּׁלשׁים ראשׁ (<hi type="italic">head of the thirty</hi>), the reading in the Chronicles, we have here השּׁלשׁי ראשׁ (<hi type="italic">head of the three</hi>). Bertheau would alter our text in accordance with the Chronicles, whilst Thenius proposes to bring the text of the Chronicles into accordance with ours. But although the many unquestionable corruptions in the verse before us may appear to favour Bertheau’s assumption, we cannot regard either of the emendations as necessary, or even warrantable. The proposed alteration of השּׁלשׁי is decidedly precluded by the recurrence of השּׁלשׁי ראשׁ in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference>, and the alteration of השּׁלשׁים in the Chronicles by the repeated allusion to the שׁלשׁים, not only in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.15">2Sa 23:15</reference>, 42; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.6">1Ch 27:6</reference> of the Chronicles, but also in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.24">2Sa 23:24</reference> of the chapter before us. The explanation given of שׁלשׁי and שׁלשׁים, as signifying chariot-warriors, is decidedly erroneous;<note placement="foot">This explanation, which we find in <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.) and Bertheau, rests upon no other authority than the testimony of Origen, to the effect that an obscure writer gives this interpretation of τριστάτης, the rendering of שׁלישׁ, an authority which is completely overthrown by the writer of the gloss in <hi type="italic">Octateuch. </hi> (Schleussner, <hi type="italic">Lex. in</hi> lxx t. v. p. 338), who gives this explanation of τριστάτας: τοὺς παρὰ χεῖρα τοῦ βασιλέως ἀριστερὰν τρίτης μοίρας ἄρχοντας. Suidas and Hesychius give the same explanation (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> τριστάται). <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> also observes (ad Ezek 23): “It is the name of the second rank next to the king.”</note> for the singular השּׁלישׁ is used in all the passages in which the word occurs to signify the royal aide-de-camp (2Ki 7:2, 2Ki 7:17, 2Ki 7:19; 2Ki 9:25; 2Ki 15:25), and the plural שׁלישׁים the royal body-guard, not only in 2Ki 15:25, but even in 1Ki 9:22, and <reference osisRef="Exod.14.7">Exo 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.4">Exo 15:4</reference>, from which the meaning chariot-warriors has been derived. Consequently השּׁלשׁי ראשׁ is the head of the king’s aides-de-camp, and the interchange of השּׁלשׁי with the השּׁלשׁים of the Chronicles may be explained on the simple ground that David’s thirty heroes formed his whole body of adjutants. The singular שׁלשׁי is to be explained in the same manner as הכּרתי (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>). Luther expresses the following opinion in his marginal gloss with regard to the words which follow (העצנו עדינו הוּא עדינו): “We believe the text to have been corrupted by a writer, probably from some book in an unknown character and bad writing, so that <hi type="italic">orer</hi> should be substituted for <hi type="italic">adino</hi>, and <hi type="italic">ha - eznib</hi> for <hi type="italic">eth hanitho :</hi>” that is to say, the reading in the Chronicles, “he swung his spear,” should be adopted (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference>). This supposition is certainly to be preferred to the attempt made by Gesenius (<hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.) and v. Dietrich (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> עדין) to find some sense in the words by assuming the existence of a verb עדּן and a noun עצן, a spear, since these words do not occur anywhere else in Hebrew; and in order to obtain any appropriate sense, it is still necessary to resort to alterations of the text. “<hi type="italic">He swung his spear over eight hundred slain at once</hi>.” This is not to be understood as signifying that he killed eight hundred men at one blow, but that in a battle he threw his spear again and again at the foe, until eight hundred men had been slain. The Chronicles give three hundred instead of eight hundred; and as that number occurs again in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference>, in the case of Abishai, it probably found its way from that verse into this in the book of Chronicles.

(Schleussner, Lex. in lxx t. v. p. 338), who gives this explanation of τριστάτας: τοὺς παρὰ χεῖρα τοῦ βασιλέως ἀριστερὰν τρίτης μοίρας ἄρχοντας. 2Sa 23:8-39
The following list of David’s heroes we also find in 1 Chron 11:10-47, and expanded at the end by sixteen names ( 1Ch 11:41-47 ), and attached in 1Ch 11:10 to the account of the conquest of the fortress of Zion by the introduction of a special heading. According to this heading, the heroes named assisted David greatly in his kingdom, along with all Israel, to make him king, from which it is evident that the chronicler intended by this heading to justify his appending the list to the account of the election of David as king over all the tribes of Israel ( 1Ch 11:1 ), and of the conquest of Zion, which followed immediately afterwards. In every other respect the two lists agree with one another, except that there are a considerable number of errors of the text, more especially in the names, which are frequently corrupt in both texts, to that the true reading cannot be determined with certainty. The heroes enumerated are divided into three classes. The first class consists of three, viz., Jashobeam , Eleazar , and Shammah , of whom certain brave deeds are related, by which they reached the first rank among David’s heroes ( 2Sa 23:8-12 ). They were followed by Abishai and Benaiah , who were in the second class, and who had also distinguished themselves above the rest by their brave deeds, though they did not come up to the first three ( 2Sa 23:18-23 ). The others all belonged to the third class, which consisted of thirty-two men, of whom no particular heroic deeds are mentioned (vv. 24-39). Twelve of these, viz., the five belonging to the first two classes and seven of the third, were appointed by David commanders of the twelve detachments into which he divided the army, each detachment to serve for one month in the year (1 Chron 27).
